blocks.text: Reed writes that Chilberg “has just returned from an extensive trip to Alaska” including Nome and “has advised me of his conference with you respecting a mastodon which is imbedded in the ice in certain place in Alaska which is known to you. President Chilberg and myself today briefly discussed the uses to which the mastodon could be put if brought here as a feature of the 1909 Exposition. The more we discussed the more favorable we became to the idea of making use of this mastodon.” Requests at Chilberg’s direction “that you kindly favor us with as full information as you possess regarding the mastodon and its condition and about what would have to be done to get it out of its present location, so that it may be shipped to Seattle to use in connection with the Exposition. I inferred from my conversation with President Chilberg that you might feel that for the present at least you would not want to disclose the place where the mastodon now is. We thought, however, that it would be agreeable to you to tell us as much as would please you concerning the state of the specimen and what condition it was in when you last saw it. We would also like to know about how many persons should accompany you to the place where the mastodon is so that we may satisfy ourselves in the matter of estimating the cost of bringing it to Seattle.”

blocks.text: “I immediately consulted my partner C.W. Graham [sic], in regard to getting the animal out and the best way to go about it. Our opinion is to get a gasoline launch and as soon as navigation opens on the Yukon for one of us to go up the river, secure and engineer and man to run it, and go up and thoroughly examine the country, and if possible dig enough ice from around the animal to ascertain as near as possible what condition the animal is in and also to try and figure out the best means of getting it out, without incurring an unnecessary expense. We have figured out several ways of getting the animal out, one was that six men go in there in the fall of 1907, build winter quarters, swamp out a road and take a horse and feed with us and all necessary tools, block and tackle and outfit; build a small barge or take one with us. Make boxes big enough to hold the skin and bones taken out in sections, cut ice to pack it with. Dig out the animal and in the spring of 1908 just before the snow goes and the breakup occurs to have the thing completed, load the barge, pack with ice and come down the river to the Yukon and on to St. Michaels and ship to Seattle. But I think that the first thing would be for me to make the trip in the spring as I have stated so as to ascertain about what to do before taking in the outfit. It would require about two months for the trip. I would return and make my report by telegraph if necessary, and we could act accordingly, it would probably save quite a little expense of handling the thing later on. The first trip would cost some money, buying a boat gasoline, wages and expenses which you could furnish here through the bank.

blocks.text: “It was discovered several years ago by an old Indian in one of his hunting trips. He died in 1900 but in 1898 and 1899 he took my partner E.W. Graham to see the animal which he found imbedded in a glacier in a kind of cavern which had been hollowed out by nature in the rocks in the hill side, the blue ice was quite thick at the time. The animal as near as he could ascertain was resting on its haunches on an angle of 15 or 20 degrees. It looked to be an extraordinary big thing, he could make out its tusk protruding from its head and look to be about 16 feet long or over. The Indian stated that one time the ice had melted enough away from the side of the animal for him to get quite a lot of the hair which according to his measurement was about 8 or 10 inches long. Mr. Graham made two trips to see the animal that winter. My trip was made in winter time in 1904. That is the reason that we want to make the trip in the spring first to find just how to go about it. The country is heavily timbered. In going in the fall I think 6 men would be enough with a good outfit. We might have to take a small boiler with us. We would leave here about September 1st 1907 and get back as soon as navigation opens in 1908. I would like to pick the men here. Men that I know that has had years of experience in this country. Could pay them wages or a stipulated sum whichever would be best.

blocks.text: “The only questions are as to the genuineness of the find, and whether complete enough to restore. We have had numerous reports of the finding of mammoth carcases in Alaska, but mostly more or less fictitious as far as we could judge, and the evidence to verify them was never forthcoming. The Smithsonian sent an expedition up there some years ago to look into such reports, but all that were investigated turned out to be based on scattered bones, which are common enough. No mammoth skeleton, much less a carcase, has yet been found in Alaska to my knowledge (I do not pretend to have kept track however of all the various reports).

blocks.text: “Professor Osborn has been investigated alleged discoveries of mammoths in Alaska for many years and has had many conversations with explorers of that country. In most cases the stories which have been brought to him have proved to be greatly exaggerated. In the case of the present specimen it hardly seems possible that it can have remained for several years partially exposed in ice without washing out and decomposing. However, the statement made by Mr. J.H. Startsman of December 30th, 1906, is so explicit that we are encouraged to hope that this animal may be completely preserved. He writes that the animal was found several years ago by an Indian who guided Mr. Graham to it in the years 1898 and 1899. Mr. Graham found it embedded in a glacier. He said the animal was partially exposed, displaying a lot of the head. Mr. Startsman visited the animal in 1904. He suggests that the trip be made in the spring of 1907 in order to find out just how the animal is preserved, and adds that the price of the specimen would be determined by the condition of it and that the expedition should return for the specimen in the fall, say September 1st, 1907, taking six men and returning as soon as navigation opens in the spring of 1908.

He suggests that the trip be made in the spring of 1907 in order to find out just how the animal is preserved, and adds that the price of the specimen would be determined by the condition of it and that the expedition should return for the specimen in the fall, say September 1<sup>st</sup>, 1907, taking six men and returning as soon as navigation opens in the spring of 1908.

blocks.text: “This leaves open the very important question of the price, which should be agreed upon in a general way beforehand x. we begin any negotiations at all and before negotiations are begun it should be distinctly agreed that we are not bidding in competition with any other institution. If the owners desire to deal with another institution they are at liberty to do so, but we make it a rule not to compete or allow our offer to be used as a means of leaving[?] bids or offers from other institutions  The museum value of the specimen depends upon its completeness and its size. If this is a very large mammoth and an absolutely complete skeleton in such preservation that it can be transported without crumbling to pieces en route from the ice it is worth $5,000. to us and we should be ready to pay that price for it. If the hide and hair are preserved complete and in such condition that considerable portions can be preserved in alcohol and brought back to the Museum, we should be prepared to add $2,500. The specimen would thus cost us $7,500. as it stands. It would probably cost us not less than $7,500. more to secure it, and the expense of securing it might run up to a much higher figure, say $10,000. If the specimen lacks portions of the feet and limbs its value would be greatly impaired. If the hide is partially preserved it would add to the value and we would make a fair allowance for that.

blocks.text: “I have had an interview with Mr. Madison Grant and Mr. Quackenbush, concerning the expedition made a year ago to Alaska in search of the Hairy Mammoth. You will remember that Mr. Quackenbush found portions of a mammoth protruding from the frozen ground; that he secured certain parts of the skeleton, together with some of the hair and wool, and that he stated that there were indications of decomposing animal tissue, which led him to believe that by careful excavating he might uncover the body of one of these animals.
blocks.html: “I have had an interview with Mr. Madison Grant and Mr. Quackenbush, concerning the expedition made a year ago to Alaska in search of the Hairy Mammoth. You will remember that Mr. Quackenbush found portions of a mammoth protruding from the frozen ground; that he secured certain parts of the skeleton, together with some of the hair and wool, and that he stated that there were indications of decomposing animal tissue, which led him to believe that by careful excavating he might uncover the body of one of these animals.
blocks.speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)

blocks.text: “It seems that the bank at which Mr. Quackenbush made his discovery is being cut away by the water, and that there are prospects of the results of his work coming to naught, unless he is equipped and sent into the field in time to take advantage of the brief warm season of the coming summer. Both Mr. Grant, who, as you know, is greatly interested in this enterprise and has made many personal sacrifices to benefit the Museum, and Mr. Quackenbush are strongly of the opinion that it would be desirable to undertake this work during the next summer, and they estimate that a fund of at least $1,500 would be necessary to put Mr. Quackenbush into the field, pay for his maintenance and expenses while there, and for his return journey to New York.

blocks.text: “The first boat to arrive at Nome in the spring is always the ‘Corwin,’ June 3rd being her earliest date of arrival. Other boats do not reach Nome until June 20th or later, though they make the trip from Seattle in less than half the time. Kotzebue Sound is blocked by ice late in the season and the Corwin’s record date of arrival at Keewalik (the final outfitting point) is July 5th. By taking passage on the ‘Corwin’ when she first leaves Seattle and allowing eight or ten days to cross Seward Peninsula by rail and on horseback from Nome, I could reach Keewalik from two weeks to one month ahead of the Corwin’s arrival. This crossing would be expensive; I do not know the exact figures but should say $200, at a guess. My idea would be to make the crossing with only bed, tent, and some provisions, leave Keewalik as soon as possible with a light outfit, and get on the ground early. I could then return later, or send a man, to Keewalik to meet the ‘Corwin’ and bring to Elephant Point whatever supplies etc. it may be found necessary to ship to Keewalik by boat.

blocks.text: “I might suggest that an exploration of the Buckland River would fit in very well in this time. A. G. Maddren (“Smithsonian Exploration in search of mammoth”) marks on his map, at a point about 50 or 75 miles up the Buckland, an area of elevated Pleistocene, lacustrine, silts and Pleistocene mammal deposit; I found bones of the mammoth, horse, bison, and caribou on the lower part of the Buckland River and heard many reports of mammoth finds higher up. If any of the fossils at Elephant Point are secondarily deposited they have probably come from the Buckland; this seems to be a promising locality and it can be explored in connection with a trip to Elephant Point at an additional expense of about $535, including wages for one man, provisions, my salaray, and the purchase and shipment of a canoe to Keewalik. A canoe is an absolute necessity on the Buckland, or any other small river, and no canoes or light rowboats are used on the Seward Peninsula; in this part of Alaska travelling is done in winter, or the prospectors use launches or work their way along very slowly with heavy boats on the large rivers and do not attempt to navigate the rapid streams. The Buckland River has never been boated by a prospector, except for a few miles, and is vastly unexplored. The canoe which I borrowed last summer is, so far as I know, the only comparatively light boat on the Seward Peninisula, but it is in very bad condition and would be unsafe to use, even if I could get it again.

blocks.text: Handwritten “Report on Alaskan Mammoth Expedition, 1908.
blocks.html: Handwritten “Report on Alaskan Mammoth Expedition, 1908.
blocks.speaker: editorial note (R. J. H. Woods)

blocks.text: “Dr. H.C. Bumpus
blocks.html: “Dr. H.C. Bumpus
blocks.speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)

blocks.text: “Dear Sir,
blocks.html: “Dear Sir,
blocks.speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)

blocks.text: “In accordance with your permission I left New York City a week earlier than the date first agreed upon (May 27th) and spent this time on the road to Seattle, charging the extra expense to my personal account. I left Seattle by steamer on June 4th and owing to very exceptional ice conditions did not reach Nome until June 21st.

I left Seattle by steamer on June 4<sup>th</sup> and owing to very exceptional ice conditions did not reach Nome until June 21<sup>st</sup>.
blocks.speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)

blocks.text: “From Nome I proceeded to the head of the Seward Peninsula R.R. at Lane’s Landing and thence crossed the peninsula by wagon to Candle. The crossing from Nome to Candle occupied four and one half days, two stops were made at settlements and the remaining two in open camp.

blocks.speaker: historical writer (as transcribed by the PI)

blocks.text: “At Candle I engaged a man to act as cook and assistant and also hired his fishing dory for cruising along the coast to Elephant Point and around Eschscholtz Bay. On June 29th we rowed down the Keewalik River to Keewalik on Kotzebue Sound. The first boat of the season did not reach Keewalik until two weeks later; she brought a canoe which I had sent by freight direct from the factory in Maine to Seattle, and thence to Home.

The first boat of the season did not reach Keewalik until two weeks later; she brought a canoe which I had sent by freight direct from the factory in Maine to Seattle, and thence to Home.

blocks.text: “On July 1st I started for Elephant Point in the dory. Kotzebue Sound and Eschscholtz Bay were still packed with ice but we fortunately found a way through and reached Elephant Point on July 3rd; the mammoth remains had not been disturbed. Excavation was commenced on the 4th, and a few days work proved that the skeleton was incomplete and that comparatively little skin and hair had been preserved. I therefore decided to finish the excavation by hand; it would have been necessary, in case of finding more complete remains, to return to Keewalik for a steam thawing apparatus and at least one other assistant.

blocks.text: “The parts found in 1907 consisted of an innominate bone and hind limb (minus some foot-bones) together with some flesh, skin, and hair; there was good reason to believe that the rest of the skeleton would be found in place but the results are somewhat disappointing. This season I found in addition, a few vertebrae and ribs; the lower jaw with the teeth; a few foot bones; the two tusks; a quantity of small skull fragments; most of the tail vertebrae, the end of the tail being encased in skin; a piece of skin three feet long, found under the innominate bone; and a small quantity of hair and wool.

blocks.text: “Having taken out the mammoth remains, examined the entire bluff, and collected a number of fossils, I crossed Eschscholtz Bay to a cut bluff on the north side near Choris Peninsula. After gathering some fossils here I returned to Keewalik, built boxes, packed the collection, and prepared for an expedition up the Buckland River which seemed the most promising locality to examine. Prospectors asserted that the Buckland River is navigable, by canoe, for 150 or 200 miles and that numerous fossils have been found along its banks. I bought provisions for forty days and left Keewalik in the day, with the canoe in tow, on July 20th. In the morning of the 22nd the dory was anchored 8 miles up the river and we took to the canoe.

Prospectors asserted that the Buckland River is navigable, by canoe, for 150 or 200 miles and that numerous fossils have been found along its banks. In the morning of the 22<sup>nd</sup> the dory was anchored 8 miles up the river and we took to the canoe.

blocks.text: “The Buckland was found to be much smaller than reports made it. The water was extremely low and numerous gravel bars were almost dry; this necessitated much portaging and made progress slow. The river runs through low, rolling, hills formed of lava which, at a point 90 miles above the mouth, overlaps sedimentary rocks. Scattered along the margin of the narrow valley are deposits of silt; one such deposit at the lower end of a broad basin – 62 miles up the river – is fully one hundred feet thick and probably once filled the entire basin to that depth. I found a number of fossils—mainly badly decayed mammoth tusks—distributed all along the river, but only isolated parts and no evidence of any special deposit of fossils. A few specimens were collected. On July 28th I reached a point estimated at 86 miles above the mouth of the river and could go no further with the canoe. I walked a few miles higher but no cut silt banks were within sight and as the river seemed about to dry up altogether I turned back. On the return trip I ascended the West Fork a few miles and on August 5th reached the mouth of the river.

blocks.text: “Here I transferred the outfit to the dory and then crossed the Buckland estuary to the extreme eastern end of Eschscholtz Bay to examine a small stream where “mud” banks were reported by Beechey in 1826, but found sand bluffs and no fossils. I next cruised along the south shore of Eschscholtz Bay from the mouth of the Buckland westward past Elephant Point to the end of the silt deposit and collected a few more fossils. On August 11th I crossed to the north shore of Eschscholtz Bay, and on the following morning, leaving the boats, we set out on foot with likght packs and crossed Hotham Peninsula to Hotham Inlet. Four days were spent in examining parts of the south shore of Selawik Lake and the southern and western shores of Hotham Inlet. High bluffs face the water all around and on Hotham Inlet there are many miles of cut silt bluffs from fifty to one hundred feet high. All these bluffs proved to be almost barren of fossils although the deposit is continuous with that on Exchscholtz Bay near CHoris Peninsula where I found as many fossils—in proportion to the area of cut bluff—as at Elephant Point. On August 17th we recrossed Hotham Peninsula to Eschscholtz Bay where we were delayed by a storm. On August 20th I returned to Keewalik.

blocks.text: “The remainder of the summer season was too short to make it worth while to attempt further collecting exploration from this place; I therefore took the first boat for Nome (on August 29th) and reached New York on September 23rd.

blocks.text: “My accounts have been handed in to the Secretary. The canoe is in good condition and was stored in the warehouse of the Keewalik Hotel together with a few tools and cooking utensils; these were all left in charge of Mr. Ferdinand Quinn (P.O. address Candle, Alaska) with an order to sell the canoe—if possible—for not less than $75.00 which he is to forward to the Museum. The remainder of the outfit was valued at $10.00.

blocks.text: “It was not a careful exploration of Coffee Creek that Doctor Matthew and I had in mind, but a careful exploration of some other region. The fact that hair was present does not in the least indicate that there was a whole mammoth attached to it. In fact, the condition of the hair shows that it had been exposed to the elements for a long time and probably everything else is gone. Peale found hair of the mastodon when he dug it up back of Newburgh, but there was not the slightest trace of hid or flesh. From the work of Gilmore, the observations of Nelson and the information that I have myself gathered, I think that the chance of getting any entire mammoth in Alaska is out of the question and to even find a complete skeleton is barely possible. All the finds so far reported come from the gravel in the old beds of creeks and have consisted merely of scattered bones, so I fear that this season at least we will have to let the mammoth go.
